title: Costs, Revenue and the Firm
bigQuestion: How does a business owner know whether making one more taco, hiring one more worker, or staying open one more month is worth it?

story.title: The Numbers on the Napkin
story.kicker: A line cook quits her job, buys a used food truck, and learns in one month that revenue and profit are not the same thing.
paragraphs: Marisol had cooked on the line at a Pilsen restaurant for six years. In March she quit, signed a loan for a used food truck, and painted Tres Hermanas on the side. Her plan was simple. She would sell three kinds of tacos at $3 each, parked near the train stops and office towers downtown. On the last night of April she sat at her kitchen table with a paper napkin and a pen and tried to find out whether the month had worked.

The good news came first. She had sold about 6,000 tacos in April. At $3 apiece, that was $18,000 coming in. She had never seen a number that large with her name on it. For a minute she felt rich. Then her sister Lupe, who keeps the books for a dentist, pulled up a chair and said, "Now write down everything that went out."

The list was longer than Marisol expected. The truck loan cost $900 a month and insurance $300. The city requires food trucks to prepare food in a licensed commissary kitchen, and her share of one was $1,200 a month. Those three bills came to $2,400 whether she sold one taco or ten thousand. Then came the costs that grew with every taco: tortillas, meat, onions, cilantro and limes at about $1.10 per taco, which was $6,600. Her helper's wages were $3,200. Propane, gasoline and paper goods added $800. The total was $13,000.

So the month's profit was $18,000 minus $13,000, or $5,000. Marisol smiled. Lupe did not. "What did the restaurant pay you?" she asked. About $4,200 a month, with health insurance. "And how many hours did you work in April?" Marisol counted: about 300. Her $5,000 had cost her a $4,200 paycheck and a lot of sleep. She was ahead, but by less than the napkin first suggested.

Before bed, Lupe asked one more question. "If you park a second truck at the ballpark, do you make twice as much?" Marisol did not know. Answering that question, it turns out, is what this chapter is about. Every idea here, from fixed costs to the profit-maximizing rule to whether to form a corporation, is already sitting on that napkin.
story.think: Marisol earned $5,000 more than she spent but gave up a $4,200 paycheck and worked 300 hours. Was April a success? What other numbers would you want before deciding?

lessons.title: Revenue Is Not Profit
lessons.mainIdea: Profit is total revenue minus total cost, and a business can bring in a lot of money and still lose.
reading: A business takes in money when it sells things and pays out money to make them. The money coming in is *revenue*. Total revenue is simply price times quantity sold. Marisol sold 6,000 tacos at $3 each, so her total revenue was 6,000 × $3 = $18,000. If a lemonade stand sells 250 cups at $2, its revenue is $500. Revenue is the first number an owner sees, and it is the one that fools people.

The money going out is *total cost*: everything the business spends to produce and sell its product. Marisol's total cost in April was $13,000. *Profit* is what is left when you subtract total cost from total revenue. Her profit was $18,000 − $13,000 = $5,000. When total cost is larger than total revenue, the difference is a *loss*. A truck that spent $13,000 but took in only $11,000 would have a loss of $2,000.

The most common mistake is to treat revenue as if it were profit. A store can double its revenue and still end the year worse off if its costs rise faster. Suppose a shop's revenue climbs from $20,000 to $22,000 in a month, but its costs climb from $15,000 to $19,000. Profit did not rise. It fell from $5,000 to $3,000. Owners who watch only the register miss this.

A higher price does not always mean higher revenue, either. If Marisol raised her price to $4 and customers responded by buying only 4,000 tacos, her revenue would be 4,000 × $4 = $16,000, which is $2,000 less than before. Price and quantity work together, and the demand curve you studied earlier decides how they trade off. Every decision in this chapter starts by asking what happens to revenue and what happens to cost.

words.d: the money a business takes in from sales; total revenue equals price times quantity sold
everything a business spends to produce and sell its product
total revenue minus total cost, when the result is positive
what a business has when total cost is greater than total revenue

look.title: Two Months, One Register
look.text: A neighborhood bakery took in $9,000 in January and $11,000 in February, so the owner told her staff that February was the better month. In January the bakery spent $6,500. In February a broken oven and higher flour prices pushed spending to $9,800.
look.prompt: Work out the profit for each month. Which month was really better, and by how much? What did the owner look at, and what did she skip?

check.q: A lemonade stand sells 250 cups at $2 each. What is its total revenue?
check.why: Total revenue is price times quantity: 250 × $2 = $500.

check.q: A food truck has total revenue of $18,000 and total cost of $13,000. What is its profit?
check.why: Profit is total revenue minus total cost: $18,000 − $13,000 = $5,000.

check.q: A shop's revenue rose from $20,000 to $22,000 while its costs rose from $15,000 to $19,000. What happened to profit?
choices: The shop now has a loss
check.why: Profit was $20,000 − $15,000 = $5,000 and became $22,000 − $19,000 = $3,000. Revenue went up, but costs went up more.

lessons.title: Fixed and Variable Costs
lessons.mainIdea: Fixed costs stay the same no matter how much you produce; variable costs rise with every unit you make.
reading: Look again at Marisol's napkin and sort the costs into two piles. The truck loan ($900), insurance ($300) and the commissary kitchen ($1,200) add up to $2,400. She owes that $2,400 in a month when she sells 6,000 tacos, and she owes it in a month when a blizzard keeps her home and she sells none. A cost that does not change with the amount produced is a *fixed cost*.

Tortillas, meat, propane and paper napkins are different. Every extra taco uses about $1.10 more of ingredients. If she sells nothing, she buys nothing. A cost that rises and falls with output is a *variable cost*. Her helper's wages count as variable too, because she schedules more hours on busy days and fewer on slow ones. Some costs can be either, depending on how the business is set up. The test is always the same: does this bill change when output changes?

Total cost is fixed cost plus variable cost. A small table shows how it grows. At 0 tacos, total cost is $2,400 + $0 = $2,400. At 1,000 tacos, variable cost is 1,000 × $1.10 = $1,100, so total cost is $3,500. At 3,000 tacos it is $2,400 + $3,300 = $5,700. Notice that each extra thousand tacos adds the same $1,100. The fixed part never moves; the variable part climbs in a straight line.

Two mistakes are common. The first is thinking fixed means small or unimportant. Fixed costs are often the biggest bills a young business faces, and they come due even in a bad month. The second is thinking fixed means forever. Economists call the period when at least one cost is fixed the *short run*. In the *long run*, everything can change: Marisol can sell the truck, drop the kitchen lease or buy a second truck. In the long run, every cost is variable.

words.d: a cost that stays the same no matter how much the business produces, such as rent or a loan payment
a cost that rises and falls with the amount produced, such as ingredients
a period in which at least one cost, such as a lease, cannot be changed
a period long enough that every cost can be changed

look.title: Total Cost as Output Grows
look.cite: Tres Hermanas food truck, a labeled example
look.prompt: What is the fixed cost in this table, and how do you know? How much does each extra taco add to total cost?

check.q: Which of these is a fixed cost for a food truck?
choices: Extra helper hours on a busy day
check.why: Insurance is owed every month whether the truck sells one taco or ten thousand. The others rise and fall with output.

check.q: Fixed cost is $2,400 and variable cost is $1.10 per taco. What is total cost at 3,000 tacos?
check.why: Variable cost is 3,000 × $1.10 = $3,300. Add the fixed $2,400 to get $5,700.

check.q: A blizzard closes the truck for a month and it sells nothing. What happens to its fixed cost?
check.why: Fixed costs such as the loan and insurance do not change with output. They are owed even at zero sales.

lessons.title: The Owner's Hidden Cost
lessons.mainIdea: Economic profit subtracts the owner's opportunity cost as well as the bills, so it is smaller than the profit on the napkin.
reading: Marisol's napkin listed every bill she paid: the loan, the kitchen, the meat, the wages. Costs that are paid out in money are *explicit costs*. But her sister spotted a cost with no receipt. To run the truck, Marisol gave up a job that paid $4,200 a month. That paycheck is the opportunity cost of her own time. A cost that is the value of something the owner already has and uses, rather than a bill, is an *implicit cost*.

This gives two ways to measure profit. *Accounting profit* is revenue minus explicit costs: $18,000 − $13,000 = $5,000. *Economic profit* also subtracts implicit costs: $5,000 − $4,200 = $800. Suppose Marisol had also pulled $10,000 out of a savings account that paid $30 a month in interest. That lost interest is another implicit cost, and economic profit falls to $770. Same truck, same month, three different numbers, each answering a different question.

Economic profit answers the question owners most need: am I doing better than my next-best option? A positive economic profit means yes. A negative one means the owner would be better off, in money terms, doing something else. Zero economic profit is not failure. It means the business pays the owner exactly what she could earn elsewhere, which economists call a normal profit. Many healthy small businesses live near zero economic profit for years.

Remember the rule from the opportunity cost chapter: the implicit cost is the single next-best alternative, not a list. Marisol gave up the restaurant job. She did not also give up a job at a hotel kitchen and a job at a bakery, because she could only have worked one of them. Counting three lost salaries would make the truck look far worse than it is. Count one, the best one.

words.d: a cost paid out in money, such as rent, wages or supplies
the value of something the owner already has and uses in the business, such as her own time or savings
total revenue minus explicit costs
total revenue minus both explicit and implicit costs

look.title: The Bike Shop on Milwaukee Avenue
look.text: Deion runs a bicycle repair shop. Last year the shop's revenue was $110,000 and his bills for rent, parts, tools and a part-time helper came to $72,000. Before opening the shop he turned down a $45,000-a-year job as a mechanic at a bus garage. He also put $20,000 of savings into the shop, money that had been earning $600 a year in interest.
look.prompt: Find Deion's accounting profit and his economic profit. Is he better off, in money terms, than he would be at the bus garage? What else might matter to him?

check.q: Which of these is an implicit cost of running a food truck?
choices: The salary the owner gave up to run the truck
The cost of tortillas and meat
check.why: An implicit cost is the value of something the owner already owns and uses, here her own time. The other three are explicit costs paid in money.

check.q: A shop has accounting profit of $38,000. The owner gave up a $45,000 job to run it. What is the economic profit?
check.why: Economic profit subtracts the implicit cost: $38,000 − $45,000 = −$7,000. The owner earns less than at the next-best job.

check.q: A business earning zero economic profit is
choices: earning as much as the owner's next-best option
losing money on its accounting books
taking in no revenue at all
check.why: Zero economic profit means revenue covers every explicit cost and the owner's opportunity cost, a normal profit. It is not a loss.

lessons.title: Total, Average and Marginal Cost
lessons.mainIdea: Average cost is total cost divided by output; marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit, and it drives decisions.
reading: A print shop in Lakeview makes custom T-shirts in batches of ten. Its fixed costs come to $60 a day. Here is its total cost at each level of *output*: 0 batches, $60; 1 batch, $80; 2 batches, $95; 3 batches, $105; 4 batches, $120; 5 batches, $140. Two more numbers can be pulled out of this list, and they answer different questions.

*Average total cost* answers how much each batch costs on average. Divide total cost by the number of batches. At 4 batches, average total cost is $120 ÷ 4 = $30 per batch. At 2 batches it is $95 ÷ 2 = $47.50. Average cost usually falls at first because the $60 of fixed cost is spread over more batches. Then it stops falling and turns up, for a reason the next lesson explains.

*Marginal cost* answers what one more batch would add to total cost. Subtract the total cost before from the total cost after. The third batch raises total cost from $95 to $105, so its marginal cost is $10. The fifth batch raises it from $120 to $140, so its marginal cost is $20. The word marginal always means the next one, the extra one, the one at the edge.

People mix these up because both are stated in dollars per batch. Average cost looks backward at everything made so far. Marginal cost looks forward at the next unit only. When the shop decides whether to take one more order, the number that matters is marginal cost, because the fixed $60 is already spent either way. Keep the two questions separate: what does each batch cost on average, and what would the next batch cost?

words.d: the amount a business produces in a period, such as batches per day
total cost divided by the number of units produced
the extra cost of producing one more unit; the change in total cost

look.title: A Print Shop's Total Cost
look.cite: Lakeview T-shirt print shop, a labeled example
look.prompt: Find the marginal cost of each batch from the first to the fifth. Then find average total cost at 3 batches and at 5. At which batch does marginal cost stop falling?

check.q: Total cost is $120 at 4 batches and $140 at 5 batches. What is the marginal cost of the fifth batch?
check.why: Marginal cost is the change in total cost: $140 − $120 = $20. ($28 is the average cost at 5 batches, a different question.)

check.q: Total cost is $120 at 4 batches. What is the average total cost per batch?
check.why: Average total cost is total cost divided by output: $120 ÷ 4 = $30.

check.q: Marginal cost is best described as
choices: the added cost of producing one more unit
check.why: Marginal always means the next unit. Marginal cost is the change in total cost when output rises by one.

lessons.title: Diminishing Returns
lessons.mainIdea: When you keep adding workers to a fixed space, each new worker eventually adds less output than the one before.
reading: Marisol's truck has one grill, one prep counter and one window. Watch what happens as she adds workers during a lunch rush. Alone, she can turn out 40 tacos an hour. With a second worker taking orders and money, output jumps to 90 an hour. A third worker, chopping and wrapping, brings it to 120. A fourth brings 135. A fifth, squeezed in by the door, brings 140. The truck still makes more tacos with each hire, but by less and less.

The extra output from one more worker is the *marginal product* of that worker. Here it is 40, then 50, then 30, then 15, then 5. It rises at first because two people can split the work sensibly. Then it falls, not because anyone is lazy, but because the grill and counter are fixed. Five people cannot all reach one grill. This pattern is the law of *diminishing returns*: when you add more of one *input* to a fixed amount of another, the marginal product eventually falls.

Diminishing returns explains why marginal cost eventually rises. Suppose each worker costs $20 an hour. The third worker adds 30 tacos for $20, about 67 cents of labor per extra taco. The fifth worker adds 5 tacos for $20, or $4 of labor per extra taco. Each extra taco gets more expensive to make, so the marginal cost curve turns upward. In the print shop, the same crowding around one press explains why marginal cost began climbing after the third batch.

Do not confuse diminishing returns with falling output. Total output kept rising in the truck all the way to five workers. Diminishing means the additions shrink, not that the total drops. Only if Marisol jammed in a sixth or seventh worker, so that people bumped into each other and dropped orders, would output actually fall. That is called negative returns, and a sensible owner never gets there.

words.d: the extra output produced by adding one more unit of an input, such as one more worker
the rule that adding more of one input to a fixed input eventually adds less and less output
anything used to produce a good or service, such as labor, a grill or a truck

look.title: One Mower, Four Cousins
look.text: A lawn-care crew owns a single riding mower and a truck. One cousin working alone finishes 5 lawns a day. Two cousins, one mowing and one trimming edges, finish 9. Three finish 12, since the third can rake and bag while the others move on. When a fourth cousin joins, the crew finishes 13 lawns, because he mostly waits for a turn on the mower.
look.prompt: Write the marginal product of each cousin. Where do diminishing returns set in, and what fixed input causes them? What could the crew buy to push the point further out?

check.q: Output is 90 tacos an hour with two workers and 120 with three. What is the marginal product of the third worker?
check.why: Marginal product is the change in output: 120 − 90 = 30 tacos.

check.q: Why does the marginal product of each new worker in the truck eventually fall?
choices: The new workers are lazier than the first ones
The truck's grill and counter are fixed, so each extra worker has less to work with
check.why: Diminishing returns come from adding a variable input (workers) to a fixed input (the truck). Crowding, not effort, is the cause.

check.q: Diminishing returns means that
choices: total output falls as workers are added
costs fall as workers are added
each added worker adds less output than the one before
check.why: Total output can still rise. What shrinks is the addition each new worker makes.

lessons.title: Economies of Scale
lessons.mainIdea: In the long run a bigger operation can often produce each unit more cheaply, up to a point where it becomes too big to manage.
reading: Diminishing returns is a short-run story: the truck is fixed. In the long run Marisol can buy a bigger truck, or two, or a restaurant. Now a new question appears. When a business grows and every input grows with it, what happens to the average cost of each unit? Often it falls. When average total cost falls as a firm gets larger, the firm has *economies of scale*.

Take two breweries as a labeled example. A small one makes 10,000 barrels a year at a total cost of $2,000,000, so each barrel costs $200 on average. A large one makes 100,000 barrels at a total cost of $12,000,000, or $120 per barrel. The big brewery is not more careful. It is cheaper per barrel for three reasons. Its large fixed costs, such as tanks and a bottling line, are spread over more barrels. Its workers can specialize in one task each. And it buys grain and bottles in bulk at lower prices.

Economies of scale explain a lot of what you see. Illinois farms have grown larger over the decades partly because a combine costs about the same to own whether it harvests 500 acres or 2,000. Big-box stores, airlines and car makers all run on the same logic. It is also why a lone food truck cannot match a chain's prices on paper goods and meat.

Bigger is not always cheaper, though. Past some size, a firm becomes hard to run. Layers of managers slow decisions, workers feel unseen, and the head office loses touch with customers. When average cost starts rising as a firm grows, it faces *diseconomies of scale*. Between the two lies a range where size makes no difference, called constant returns to scale. The best size for a business is wherever its long-run average cost is lowest, and that differs by industry: small for barbers, huge for airplane makers.

words.d: falling average cost per unit as a firm grows larger
rising average cost per unit when a firm grows too large to manage well
a range of sizes where growing larger leaves average cost unchanged

look.title: The Pin Factory
look.text: Adam Smith described a pin workshop in which ten workers split the job into about eighteen separate steps. One drew out the wire, another straightened it, a third cut it, a fourth sharpened the point, and others made and attached the heads. Working this way, he estimated, the ten could make about 48,000 pins a day. Working alone, each might not have managed even twenty.
look.cite: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 1, 1776 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Smith's factory shows one source of economies of scale. Which one? Why would a workshop with two workers not be able to do the same thing?

check.q: Economies of scale means that
choices: average cost rises as output grows
average cost falls as the firm grows larger
check.why: Economies of scale is the long-run fall in average total cost as a firm gets bigger, from spreading fixed costs, specialization and bulk buying.

check.q: Plant A makes 10,000 units for $2,000,000. Plant B makes 100,000 units for $12,000,000. Which statement is right?
choices: Plant A has the lower average cost
Both plants have the same average cost
Plant B's average cost is $120, lower than Plant A's $200

check.q: Diseconomies of scale happen mainly because
choices: a very large firm becomes hard to manage and coordinate
check.why: Past some size, layers of management and poor communication push average cost back up. Discounts and specialization are reasons for economies, not diseconomies.

lessons.title: Marginal Revenue Equals Marginal Cost
lessons.mainIdea: Produce every unit whose marginal revenue is at least its marginal cost, and stop where the two are equal.
reading: How many tacos should Marisol make in a day? Not as many as possible, and not the number that makes the average cost lowest. The answer comes from comparing two margins, one unit at a time. *Marginal revenue* is the extra revenue from selling one more unit. Marisol is a small seller in a crowded downtown lunch market, so she can sell as many tacos as she makes at the going price of $3. Each extra taco brings in $3, so her marginal revenue is $3.

Now line that up against marginal cost. Because of diminishing returns, marginal cost rises as the day gets busier. Suppose the 100th taco of the day costs $1.50 to make, the 200th costs $2.00, the 300th costs $2.60, the 400th costs $3.00 and the 500th costs $3.60. The 300th taco earns $3 and costs $2.60, so it adds 40 cents of profit. Make it. The 500th earns $3 but costs $3.60, so it loses 60 cents. Do not make it.

This is the *profit-maximizing rule*: keep producing as long as marginal revenue is above marginal cost, and stop where they are equal. Marisol should make about 400 tacos a day. Making fewer leaves profitable tacos unmade. Making more adds tacos that cost more than they bring in. The rule works for a farm deciding how many acres to plant and a factory deciding how many shifts to run. It is the heart of what economists call *marginal analysis*: decide at the edge, one unit at a time.

Two mistakes are common. Some owners try to maximize profit per unit, which would mean making very few tacos and missing all the profit on the rest. Others try to maximize revenue by selling as many as possible, which means making tacos that lose money. If the going price rose to $3.60, the rule would tell Marisol to move out to 500 tacos, because the 500th now breaks even. If the price fell to $2.60, she should pull back to 300. The rule does not change; the answer does.

words.d: the extra revenue from selling one more unit; for a small seller at a set price, it equals the price
produce up to the point where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
making a decision by comparing the extra benefit and the extra cost of one more unit

look.title: Marginal Cost as the Day Gets Busy
look.cite: Tres Hermanas food truck, a labeled example
look.prompt: At a price of $3, how many tacos should the truck make? What if a rival opened and the price fell to $2.60? What if a festival pushed it to $3.60?

check.q: The price is $3 and the 500th taco has a marginal cost of $3.60. Should Marisol make it?
choices: No, it adds $3.60 in cost but only $3 in revenue
No, because marginal cost is below the price
check.why: Compare margins: the 500th taco loses $0.60. Revenue rises, but cost rises more, so profit falls.

check.q: A small seller can sell all it wants at $3 each. What is its marginal revenue?
choices: It falls with each taco sold
check.why: Each extra unit sold at the going price adds exactly that price to revenue, so marginal revenue is $3.

check.q: The profit-maximizing rule says a firm should
choices: produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
produce where average cost is lowest
produce as much as it possibly can
produce where the price is highest
check.why: Every unit with marginal revenue above marginal cost adds profit; every unit beyond the point where they are equal subtracts profit.

lessons.title: Break-Even and Shutdown
lessons.mainIdea: A firm breaks even when revenue covers all costs, and it should stay open in a bad month as long as revenue covers its variable costs.
reading: Lupe asked Marisol a fair question: how many tacos do you have to sell just to cover your costs? That number is the *break-even point*, where total revenue equals total cost. Each taco sells for $3 and uses $1.10 of variable cost, so each taco leaves $1.90 to put toward the $2,400 of fixed costs. Divide: $2,400 ÷ $1.90 is about 1,263. Marisol must sell roughly 1,264 tacos a month before she earns her first dollar of profit. Below that she loses; above it she gains $1.90 per taco.

Now picture a slow winter month. Marisol sells only 1,000 tacos, for $3,000 in revenue. Her variable costs are 1,000 × $1.10 = $1,100, and her fixed costs are still $2,400. Total cost is $3,500, so she loses $500. Should she close for the month? Compare the loss from staying open to the loss from closing. If she closes, she still owes the $2,400 of fixed costs and takes in nothing, so she loses $2,400. Open, she loses only $500. Open is better.

The reason is that revenue of $3,000 more than covers the variable cost of $1,100, leaving $1,900 to chip away at the fixed bills. This is the *shutdown rule*. In the short run, stay open as long as price is at least *average variable cost*, the variable cost per unit. Here average variable cost is $1.10 and the price is $3. Only if the price fell below $1.10, so that each taco lost money on ingredients alone, would closing be the smaller loss.

The break-even point and the shutdown point answer different questions. Break-even asks when the business earns a profit; it includes fixed costs. Shutdown asks whether to operate at all this month; it ignores fixed costs because they are owed either way. In the long run, a business that never reaches break-even should leave the industry, since the lease will eventually end and the truck can be sold. But in the short run, many businesses correctly stay open while losing money.

words.d: the level of sales at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero
variable cost divided by the number of units produced
in the short run, keep operating as long as price covers average variable cost, because fixed costs are owed either way

look.title: The Snowplow in a Mild Winter
look.text: Kenji owns a pickup with a plow and clears parking lots for $60 each. His truck loan and insurance cost $1,500 a month no matter what. Each lot he plows uses about $15 of fuel and salt. This January it barely snowed, and he expects to plow only 40 lots.
look.prompt: Work out Kenji's revenue, variable cost and total loss for January if he keeps plowing. What would he lose if he parked the truck instead? Should he plow this month? How many lots does he need to break even?

check.q: Fixed cost is $2,400 a month, the price is $3 and variable cost is $1.10 per taco. About how many tacos must be sold to break even?
check.why: Each taco contributes $3 − $1.10 = $1.90 toward fixed costs. $2,400 ÷ $1.90 is about 1,263, so the 1,264th taco is the first to earn profit. Dividing $2,400 by $1.10 forgets the price.

check.q: In a slow month the truck earns $3,000, has variable costs of $1,100 and fixed costs of $2,400. Should it stay open?
choices: Yes; revenue covers variable costs and pays part of the fixed costs, so the loss is smaller open than closed
No, because it is losing money
No, because closing makes the fixed costs disappear
Yes, because it earns a $1,900 profit
check.why: Open, the loss is $500. Closed, the loss is the full $2,400 of fixed costs. Staying open is the smaller loss.

check.q: In the short run, a firm should shut down when
choices: price is below average total cost
price is below average variable cost
profit is lower than last year
check.why: If price does not even cover the variable cost of each unit, every unit made deepens the loss. Fixed costs do not matter for this choice because they are owed either way.

lessons.title: Sole Proprietors and Partners
lessons.mainIdea: A sole proprietorship is easy to start and keeps all the profit, but the owner risks everything; a partnership shares both.
reading: When Marisol started, she did not fill out any special form to become a business. She just was one. A business owned and run by one person is a *sole proprietorship*. It is the most common form of business in the United States by count: most businesses are one-person operations, from barbers to freelance coders to farm stands. Yet all of them together bring in a small share of total business sales, because each one is small.

The advantages are real. A sole proprietor decides everything, keeps every dollar of profit, and pays tax on that profit once, as personal income. The disadvantages are just as real. The biggest is *unlimited liability*: the business and the owner are legally the same, so if the truck is in an accident and a court awards $200,000, Marisol's savings, car and home can be taken to pay it. A sole proprietor also finds it hard to raise money, and the business ends when the owner quits or dies.

A *partnership* is a business owned by two or more people who share profits and decisions under an agreement. If Lupe joins Marisol, the truck gains Lupe's bookkeeping skill and her savings, and both sisters share the workload. Law firms, medical practices and many family businesses are partnerships. The cost is shared control: if one sister wants a second truck and the other does not, someone loses. And in an ordinary partnership, each general partner has unlimited liability for the debts of the whole business, even debts the other partner ran up.

The choice between these forms is a trade-off, like every choice in this course. Going alone buys speed and control at the price of risk and limited money. Partnering buys money and skills at the price of shared control and shared exposure. The next lesson shows a third form that changes the liability problem entirely.

words.d: a business owned and run by one person, who keeps the profit and bears all the risk
a business owned by two or more people who share profits, decisions and risk under an agreement
the owner's personal property can be taken to pay the business's debts

look.title: Should Lupe Join?
look.text: Lupe offers to invest $15,000 in the truck and handle the books and permits in exchange for one-third of the profit. Marisol would keep two-thirds and the final say on the menu, but the sisters would share the loan and any debts. The $15,000 would let Marisol buy a second grill and hire a second helper, which she thinks would add about $1,800 a month in profit.
look.prompt: List what Marisol gains and what she gives up if she says yes. Using the numbers, is her own monthly share likely to rise or fall? What risks does Lupe take on?

check.q: What is the main risk of running a business as a sole proprietorship?
choices: Unlimited liability: the owner's personal property can be taken to pay business debts
The owner must pay tax on profits twice
The owner cannot keep the profits
check.why: In a sole proprietorship the owner and the business are legally the same, so business debts are the owner's debts.

check.q: Which form of business is the most common in the United States, counted by number of businesses?
check.why: Most U.S. businesses are one-owner operations, though corporations bring in most of the total sales.

check.q: Compared with a sole proprietorship, a partnership offers
choices: lower taxes than any other form
more money and more skills combined in one business
check.why: Partners pool savings and abilities. They still face unlimited liability and shared control.

lessons.title: Corporations and LLCs
lessons.mainIdea: A corporation is a legal person separate from its owners, which limits their risk and lets it raise money by selling stock.
reading: A *corporation* is a business that the law treats as a person of its own, separate from the people who own it. It can own property, sign contracts, borrow, sue and be sued in its own name. Its owners hold shares of *stock*, and each share is a slice of ownership. A small corporation might have three shareholders; a giant one might have millions. In Illinois, a corporation comes into being when its founders file papers with the Secretary of State.

The great advantage is *limited liability*. If a corporation is sued or goes broke, its shareholders can lose what they paid for their shares, but no more. Their homes and savings are safe. That protection makes people willing to invest in businesses they do not run, which is the second advantage: a corporation can raise large sums by selling stock to many investors or by borrowing through bonds. A corporation also has unlimited life. Shareholders come and go, but the company goes on.

The disadvantages are cost and taxes. Setting up and running a corporation means more paperwork, more rules and more reporting. And profits can be taxed twice: the corporation pays corporate income tax on its earnings, and when it pays some of those earnings to shareholders as a *dividend*, the shareholders pay income tax on that too. Owners also share control. Shareholders elect a board of directors, and the board hires managers, so a founder can be outvoted or even fired.

Many small businesses now choose a middle path, the *limited liability company*, or LLC. An LLC gives its owners limited liability like a corporation, but its profits are normally taxed only once, on the owners' personal returns, like a proprietorship or partnership. It is simpler to run than a corporation. For Marisol, forming an LLC would mean that a lawsuit over the truck could reach the truck and the business's bank account, but not her home. Most economists would say that protection is worth the filing fee.

words.d: a business the law treats as a separate legal person, owned by shareholders
shares of ownership in a corporation
owners can lose only what they invested, not their personal property
a payment of part of a corporation's profit to its shareholders
a business form (LLC) with the liability protection of a corporation and the single taxation of a partnership

look.title: Paperwork or Protection
look.text: A lawyer tells Marisol that forming an LLC will cost a few hundred dollars in fees and a few hours a year of extra paperwork. In exchange, if a customer sues over food poisoning or the truck causes a crash, the most she can lose is what the business owns. Her house, which she shares with her mother, would be out of reach. Her friend who runs a dog-walking business says he never bothered.
look.prompt: Compare the costs and the benefits of forming the LLC for Marisol. Why might the dog walker reach a different answer than a food-truck owner? What role does risk play in each case?

check.q: Limited liability means that
choices: the owners can lose only what they invested in the business
the stock can never lose value
check.why: If the business fails or is sued, shareholders' personal property is protected. Their shares can still become worthless.

check.q: What does double taxation of a corporation refer to?
choices: Paying sales tax and income tax
Paying tax in two different years
Corporate profits are taxed, and dividends paid from them are taxed again as shareholder income
A tax on every stock purchase
check.why: The corporation pays tax on its earnings, and shareholders pay income tax on the dividends they receive from those same earnings.

check.q: Why can a corporation usually raise money more easily than a sole proprietorship?
choices: Banks are required to lend to it
It pays no interest on loans
It can sell shares of stock to many investors who risk only what they pay
check.why: Limited liability makes strangers willing to invest, so a corporation can pool money from many shareholders and bondholders.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurs and Risk
lessons.mainIdea: An entrepreneur combines resources, takes on risk, and is paid in profit if the idea works and loss if it does not.
reading: Land, labor and capital do not organize themselves into a food truck. Someone has to spot the chance, borrow the money, sign the lease, hire the helper and decide what goes on the menu. That person is the *entrepreneur*, the fourth factor of production. The entrepreneur's special job is to bear *risk*. The helper gets paid every Friday whether April was good or bad. Marisol gets paid only if there is something left after everyone else.

Profit is the entrepreneur's reward for taking that risk and for getting the combination right. It is also a signal to everyone else. When food trucks in a neighborhood earn high profits, other cooks notice and open trucks of their own. The new supply pushes prices and profits down toward normal. When trucks lose money, some close, supply falls and prices recover. Profit and loss steer resources toward what people want and away from what they do not, without anyone in charge.

The risk is not a figure of speech. Government data show that roughly half of new businesses in the United States are still operating five years after they open. The other half close, often taking the founder's savings with them. Chicago's history is full of both outcomes. Cyrus McCormick moved his reaper factory to the city in 1847 and built one of the largest firms in the world; countless other Chicago ventures vanished without a trace.

Entrepreneurs also drive *innovation*, the introduction of new products and better ways of making old ones. A new app, a cheaper solar panel or a faster way to wrap a taco all begin as somebody's risky bet. Economies with many entrepreneurs tend to grow faster because more bets are placed and the winners spread. Not everyone should start a business; the numbers say most should not. But an economy needs the ones who do.

words.d: a person who organizes land, labor and capital into a business and bears the risk of loss
the chance that a decision turns out worse than expected, including losing the money invested
a new product, or a new and better way of producing one

look.title: Two Ways to Spend $30,000
look.text: Priya has $30,000 in savings and a steady $52,000-a-year job. She can keep the job and the savings, or quit and open a mobile phone-repair kiosk in a suburban mall. She estimates a 50% chance the kiosk earns her $70,000 a year, a 30% chance it earns about $45,000, and a 20% chance it fails within a year and she loses the $30,000.
look.prompt: What does Priya risk, and what could she gain? Who bears the loss if the kiosk fails, and who collects the profit if it succeeds? Would you take the bet? What would change your answer?

check.q: What is the entrepreneur's payment for taking on risk?
check.why: Wages go to labor, interest to lenders and rent to landowners. Profit, which can be negative, is what remains for the entrepreneur.

check.q: According to the reading, roughly what share of new U.S. businesses are still operating five years after opening?
check.why: Government data show roughly half survive five years. The other half close, which is the risk the entrepreneur bears.

check.q: When businesses in an industry earn high profits, what usually happens next?
choices: New firms enter, supply rises and prices fall toward normal
Costs for buyers rise for good
check.why: Profit is a signal. It attracts new sellers, which shifts supply right and pushes price and profit back down.

lessons.title: A Chicago Print Shop, Start to Finish
lessons.mainIdea: Every idea in this chapter can be applied in order to one real-feeling business to decide whether to grow.
reading: Put the whole chapter to work on one business, a labeled example. Nadia runs a small screen-printing shop in Chicago's Lakeview neighborhood that prints custom T-shirts for schools, teams and bars. Her fixed costs are $4,000 a month: rent, the lease on her press, insurance and a website. Each shirt uses about $6 of blank shirt and ink, her variable cost. She charges $15 a shirt. Her *startup costs* two years ago, mostly the press and a deposit, were $22,000, which she has already paid; they are sunk and do not enter today's decisions.

First, the margin. Each shirt brings in $15 and costs $6 to make, leaving a *margin* of $9 to cover fixed costs and then become profit. Break-even is $4,000 ÷ $9, about 445 shirts a month. In a typical month Nadia sells 900 shirts. Revenue is 900 × $15 = $13,500. Variable cost is 900 × $6 = $5,400, so total cost is $9,400 and accounting profit is $4,100. She gave up a $3,500-a-month job to do this, so her economic profit is about $600. She is doing a little better than her next-best option, and she gets to be her own boss.

Now the growth question. A second press would raise her fixed costs to $5,500 a month, but it would let her print faster and buy blanks in larger lots, cutting variable cost to $5 a shirt. Her margin would rise to $10 and her new break-even would be $5,500 ÷ $10 = 550 shirts. If sales stayed at 900, profit would be 900 × $10 − $5,500 = $3,500, which is worse than today. The second press only pays if it brings more orders. At 1,200 shirts a month, profit would be 1,200 × $10 − $5,500 = $6,500, a clear gain.

So the decision turns on one estimate: can she sell more than 960 shirts a month with the second press? At 960 shirts, 960 × $10 − $5,500 = $4,100, exactly what she earns today. Notice how she got there. She separated fixed from variable cost, ignored the sunk startup cost, computed the margin and the break-even, subtracted her opportunity cost, and compared the extra revenue of growing with its extra cost. She also has to watch *cash flow*, since the new press must be paid for before the new orders arrive. That is the economic way of thinking applied to a Tuesday afternoon.

words.d: the one-time spending needed to open a business, such as equipment and deposits
the price of a unit minus its variable cost; the amount each sale contributes toward fixed costs and profit
the timing of money coming in and going out; a profitable business can still run short of cash

look.title: Monthly Profit with One Press
look.cite: Lakeview screen-printing shop, a labeled example
look.prompt: Check two rows by computing shirts × $9 − $4,000. Where does the shop cross from loss to profit? Then compute profit at 1,200 shirts with the second press (margin $10, fixed cost $5,500) and compare.

check.q: Fixed cost is $4,000, price is $15 and variable cost is $6 a shirt. About how many shirts does the shop need to break even each month?
check.why: Each shirt contributes $15 − $6 = $9. $4,000 ÷ $9 is about 444.4, so 445 shirts. Dividing by $15 or by $6 alone gives the wrong answers.

check.q: At 900 shirts, with revenue of $13,500 and total cost of $9,400, what is the shop's accounting profit?
check.why: Profit is revenue minus total cost: $13,500 − $9,400 = $4,100. ($8,100 is the total margin before fixed costs are paid.)

check.q: A second press raises fixed cost to $5,500 but cuts variable cost to $5 a shirt at a $15 price. What is the new break-even?
check.why: The new margin is $15 − $5 = $10 per shirt, so break-even is $5,500 ÷ $10 = 550 shirts.

review.q: Which formula gives a business's profit?
review.why: Profit is what remains from revenue after all costs are subtracted. Price times quantity is revenue, not profit.

review.q: Which of these is a variable cost for a bakery?
choices: The loan payment on the ovens
review.why: Flour use rises and falls with the number of loaves baked. Rent, insurance and loan payments are fixed.

review.q: Total cost rises from $500 to $530 when output rises from 10 units to 11. What is the marginal cost of the 11th unit?
review.why: Marginal cost is the change in total cost: $530 − $500 = $30. ($48.18 is the average cost at 11 units.)

review.q: Which observation is evidence of economies of scale?
choices: Marginal cost rises as the day gets busier
A store loses money in a slow month
Each new worker adds less output than the last
Average cost falls from $10 to $7 a unit when the plant doubles in size
review.why: Economies of scale means average cost per unit falls as the firm grows larger in the long run.

review.q: The next unit a firm could make has a marginal revenue of $8 and a marginal cost of $6. What should the firm do?
choices: Make it; it adds $2 to profit
Skip it; any cost reduces profit
Stop producing; the price is too low
review.why: As long as marginal revenue is above marginal cost, one more unit raises profit. Here it adds $8 − $6 = $2.

review.q: A business has accounting profit of $60,000. The owner's implicit costs are $50,000. What is the economic profit?
review.why: Economic profit subtracts implicit costs from accounting profit: $60,000 − $50,000 = $10,000.

review.q: A small-business owner wants limited liability but wants profits taxed only once, on her personal return. Which form fits best?
review.why: An LLC combines the liability protection of a corporation with single taxation. Proprietorships and general partnerships leave the owner fully liable.

review.q: Which statement about diminishing returns is correct?
choices: It happens because later workers are less skilled
It happens only in the long run
It occurs when more workers are added to a fixed input, such as one kitchen
review.why: Diminishing returns is a short-run pattern caused by crowding a fixed input. Total output still rises, just by less each time.
